rules.statement: Never read a client secret or private key from appsettings or other plain configuration values; load it through the secrets subsystem (key rings / secret providers).
rules.why: Secrets from the secrets subsystem can rotate and be backed by a key-management service; secrets in appsettings cannot.
rules.check: Look for client secrets, private keys or signing material bound from IConfiguration/options string values instead of a secrets/key-ring provider.

rules.statement: Every OAuth authorization-code request must use PKCE with S256 and a freshly generated state and nonce.
rules.why: PKCE binds the code to the initiator, and fresh state and nonce defend against CSRF and token replay.
rules.check: Check authorization-request builders for a missing code_challenge, a plain challenge method, or state/nonce values that are reused or not freshly random.

rules.statement: When the provider advertises authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported, require the authorization response's iss parameter to equal the expected issuer before exchanging the code.
rules.why: RFC 9207 iss checking defends against mix-up attacks.
rules.check: Look for callback handling that exchanges the code without comparing the iss response parameter to the transaction's issuer.

rules.statement: When validating an ID token, logout token or other provider-issued JWT, never accept alg none or symmetric algorithms, and validate under an explicit algorithm allow-list.
rules.why: Accepting none or symmetric algorithms lets an attacker forge tokens.
rules.check: Look for JWT validation that doesn't restrict algorithms, accepts none, or allows HS* algorithms for provider-signed tokens.

rules.statement: An ID token must be checked for iss equal to the discovered issuer, aud containing the client_id, azp when present, exp, iat, nonce, and auth_time when max_age was requested.
rules.why: These checks are what OpenID Connect Core requires for an ID token to be trusted.
rules.check: Look for ID-token validation code that skips any of these claim checks.

rules.statement: Compare token hashes, guards, synchronizer tokens and other secret values in constant time (e.g. CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals), never with ordinary string or sequence equality.
rules.why: Ordinary comparisons leak timing information about the secret.
rules.check: Look for ==, string.Equals or SequenceEqual comparing at_hash/c_hash/s_hash, logout guards, CSRF tokens or similar secret values.

rules.statement: Consume a single-use record (login transaction, state, one-time code) with one atomic take operation (read-and-delete), never a get followed by a separate delete.
rules.why: A separate get and delete lets a second request on another replica use the same record.
rules.check: Look for a get then remove on shared state for single-use values instead of an atomic take/GETDEL.

rules.statement: Take a post-login return URL from the server-side login record where it was allow-listed, never from the callback query.
rules.why: Reading it from the callback lets an attacker redirect the user to an open-redirect target.
rules.check: Look for callback handlers that read a returnUrl/redirect parameter from the request instead of the stored transaction.

rules.statement: Validate a return URL so it is relative and starts with exactly one '/', and reject it if it contains '//', a backslash, a scheme or a '..' segment; after normalization it must equal an allow-listed entry or extend one at a segment boundary.
rules.why: These rules stop open redirects through return URLs.
rules.check: Look for return-URL validation that only checks a prefix without segment boundaries, allows '//' or backslashes, or accepts absolute URLs.

rules.statement: On successful login always mint a new session handle and delete any session the old cookie pointed to; never adopt a handle the browser presented.
rules.why: Adopting a presented handle allows session fixation.
rules.check: Look for login completion that reuses an existing cookie value or session id.

rules.statement: Classify a failure by a machine-readable failure code set where the failure is detected, never by matching on exception or error message text.
rules.why: Message text is not a stable contract, so a reason picked from it breaks silently.
rules.check: Look for code that inspects Message strings or error descriptions (Contains, StartsWith) to decide a failure reason.

rules.statement: Session cookies must use a __Host- prefixed name, Secure, HttpOnly, Path=/, no Domain, and a SameSite of Strict or Lax, never None.
rules.why: The __Host- prefix and these attributes stop sibling subdomains from fixing or reading the session, and SameSite blocks cross-site requests.
rules.check: Look at CookieOptions/CookieBuilder for session or antiforgery cookies that set Domain, a Path other than /, SameSite=None, or omit Secure/HttpOnly or the __Host- prefix.

rules.statement: Never log, store or emit as telemetry a session handle, cookie value or token; store session records only under a derived hash of the handle.
rules.why: With only hashes and ciphertext in the store, a dump of the store is useless without the browser's cookie.
rules.check: Look for log calls, telemetry tags, or store keys that include raw handles, cookie values, access/refresh/ID tokens.

rules.statement: Never return tokens from an endpoint, and never keep them in HttpContext.Items or other state that outlives the request.
rules.why: Tokens must live only in the encrypted session payload and in memory during a request.
rules.check: Look for responses that serialize token values, or token values stashed in HttpContext.Items, static caches or long-lived fields.

rules.statement: When the session or shared-state store fails, fail closed with 503; never treat the request as unauthenticated (401).
rules.why: A 401 on a broken store sends the client into a login loop and hides the outage.
rules.check: Look for catch blocks around store access that return 401, an anonymous principal or a sign-out.

rules.statement: Refresh a rotating refresh token single-flight across replicas, and never retry a refresh with the old refresh token after another caller may have used it.
rules.why: Presenting a rotated refresh token twice looks like theft, and the provider revokes the whole token family.
rules.check: Look for refresh code without a per-session lock and cross-replica lease, or retry loops that resend the same refresh token.

rules.statement: Once a refresh lease is won, don't let the incoming request's cancellation token cancel the token request or the write-back of the rotated refresh token; bound them by the client's request timeout instead.
rules.why: Dropping a rotated refresh token makes the next refresh a reuse, which revokes the family.
rules.check: Look for HttpContext.RequestAborted or the request's CancellationToken passed into the refresh grant call or into persisting its result.

rules.statement: Release a distributed lease or lock only by compare-and-remove against the caller's own random owner token, never with an unconditional delete.
rules.why: An unconditional delete can release a lease another replica holds after the first one's lease expired.
rules.check: Look for lease/lock release code that calls a plain remove without checking the stored owner value.

rules.statement: An API endpoint answers an authentication challenge with 401 and a forbid with 403 as application/problem+json, never a 302 redirect to a login page.
rules.why: An API caller (fetch/XHR) can't follow a login redirect, and the SPA relies on 401 to mean no session.
rules.check: Look for API endpoints or authentication handlers that redirect on challenge or forbid.

rules.statement: A forwarding proxy must forward only to configured destinations, never derive the host from the request, and reject paths with dot segments, encoded slashes (%2F, %5C), backslashes, or anything that escapes the destination base path.
rules.why: Deriving the host or allowing path traversal turns the proxy into an SSRF or open-forwarding vector.
rules.check: Look for forwarders that build the destination URL from request host/path without allow-listing and normalization checks.

rules.statement: When forwarding to an upstream API, strip the inbound Cookie, Authorization, DPoP, anti-forgery and forwarding headers, drop upstream Set-Cookie headers, and never follow upstream redirects.
rules.why: Otherwise the browser's credentials leak upstream and an upstream API can plant cookies on the host's origin.
rules.check: Look for forwarding code or handler configuration that copies all request headers, passes Set-Cookie through, or leaves AllowAutoRedirect/UseCookies enabled.

rules.statement: Build any absolute URL the server publishes or compares (redirect_uri, post_logout_redirect_uri, issuer-like URLs) from a configured public origin, never from the request's Host or a forwarded header.
rules.why: The request's Host and forwarded headers are attacker-controlled.
rules.check: Look for Request.Host, Request.Scheme or X-Forwarded-* used to compose published or compared absolute URLs.

rules.statement: Responses from authentication and session endpoints (login, callback, user probe, logout, back-channel logout) must send Cache-Control: no-store.
rules.why: Session and token-related responses must never be cached.
rules.check: Look for new or changed auth/session endpoints whose responses don't set Cache-Control: no-store.

rules.statement: A library must not register a CORS policy on its own, and a CORS policy that allows credentials must list explicit origins, never '*'.
rules.why: CORS denies by default and is part of the CSRF defense, so a wildcard with credentials would defeat it.
rules.check: Look for AddCors/UseCors in library code, or policies with AllowAnyOrigin/SetIsOriginAllowed(_ => true) together with AllowCredentials.

rules.statement: Logout must be a POST with a synchronizer guard compared in constant time against the session; never accept a GET logout.
rules.why: A GET or unguarded logout lets a cross-site or same-site page log the user out.
rules.check: Look for logout endpoints mapped to GET or that end the session without checking a guard value.

rules.statement: Record a back-channel logout token's jti as handled only after the sessions have been ended, and answer 400 when ending them fails so the provider retries.
rules.why: Recording the jti first would make the provider's retry look like a replay, so the sessions would stay open.
rules.check: Look for jti replay recording that happens before the session-termination work completes, or a 200 returned on failure.

rules.statement: A back-channel logout token must carry the backchannel-logout event in events, contain sid or sub, contain no nonce, have typ logout+jwt when typed, and pass the same signature, iss, aud and iat checks as other provider JWTs.
rules.why: OpenID Connect Back-Channel Logout 1.0 requires these checks so that a logout token can't be confused with an ID token.
rules.check: Look for logout-token validation missing the events, nonce-absence, sid/sub or typ checks.

rules.statement: Telemetry tags must be low-cardinality constants (operation, result, reason, error type) and never carry subjects, handles, tokens, client ids or paths.
rules.why: High-cardinality or sensitive tag values blow up metric storage and leak identifiers.
rules.check: Look at metric/activity tag additions for user ids, client ids, URLs/paths, tokens or other unbounded values.

rules.statement: Log through source-generated LoggerMessage methods rather than ad hoc ILogger extension calls.
rules.why: The family's logs are source-generated by convention.
rules.check: Look for logger.LogInformation/LogWarning(...) calls with message templates instead of [LoggerMessage] partial methods.

rules.statement: Model extensible reason names and similar vocabularies as open string constants, not closed enums, unless the set is provably closed.
rules.why: With open vocabularies a new reason never breaks a consumer.
rules.check: Look for new enums representing failure reasons, event reasons or strategy names that consumers or extensions could extend.

rules.statement: Validate options at startup with ValidateOnStart, and reject any strategy or provider name that isn't registered, failing startup instead of at first use.
rules.why: Misconfiguration must fail loudly at startup, and every strategy validates its own options.
rules.check: Look for new options without validators/ValidateOnStart, or named-strategy lookups that only fail at request time.

rules.statement: Require https for configured authorities, public origins and upstream destinations outside the Development environment.
rules.why: Plain http endpoints would expose tokens and cookies in transit.
rules.check: Look for URL options whose validation doesn't refuse non-https schemes outside Development.

rules.statement: When more than one candidate (such as two selection rules) matches a request, fail closed with an exception instead of silently picking one.
rules.why: Picking one arbitrarily could bind the request to the wrong client or session namespace.
rules.check: Look for selection or resolution code that takes FirstOrDefault over multiple matches without detecting ambiguity.

rules.statement: An extension seam that gates a security decision, such as a login gate or session validator, may only reject or end the session, never skip or weaken a built-in check.
rules.why: No seam may break invariants such as callback binding, cookie attributes, CSRF checks, allow-lists or the logout guard.
rules.check: Look for gate/validator contracts or call sites that let a result bypass or override built-in validation.

rules.statement: Read private key material such as PEM files through sensitive buffers that are cleared after use, not through ordinary strings or byte arrays left for the GC.
rules.why: Key material must not linger in managed memory.
rules.check: Look for File.ReadAllText/ReadAllBytes of private keys, or key bytes kept in plain arrays that are never zeroed.
